claims.evidence: This claim is supported by memory activation data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The finding of greater memory activation in the DM condition than the RM condition qualitatively captures the finding from Chen et al., 2016 that hippocampal-neocortical coupling was stronger in the DM condition than the RM condition.
claims.source: Importantly, the finding (in the model) of greater memory activation in the DM condition than the RM condition qualitatively captures the finding from Chen et al., 2016 that the putative fMRI signature of episodic retrieval (hippocampal-neocortical coupling) was stronger in the DM condition than the RM condition.
claims.evidence: This claim compares model results to empirical findings from the cited study.

claims.claim: In the simulation, the set of available episodic memories in the RM and the DM condition is the same.
claims.source: Note that, in our simulation, the set of available episodic memories in the RM and the DM condition is the same.
claims.evidence: This claim describes a property of the simulation design.

claims.claim: In the RM condition, the network has a fully-specified situation model actively maintained in its working memory during part 2, which is sufficient for the network to predict the upcoming state.
claims.source: The main difference is that, in the RM condition, the network has a fully-specified situation model actively maintained in its working memory (the recurrent activity of the LSTM) during part 2, which is sufficient for the network to predict the upcoming state.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the model's internal state in the RM condition.

claims.claim: At the beginning of the DM condition, the network's ongoing situation model is empty – the values for all features are unknown.
claims.source: In contrast, at the beginning of the DM condition, the network's ongoing situation model is empty – the values for all features are unknown.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the model's internal state in the DM condition.

claims.claim: The learned retrieval policy is demand-sensitive.
claims.source: Overall, this result suggests that the learned retrieval policy is demand-sensitive
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the pattern of results across conditions.

claims.claim: The model sets the EM gate to a higher value in the DM and NM conditions (where there are gaps in the model's understanding) and suppresses episodic retrieval in the RM condition (where there are no gaps).
claims.source: We found that the model sets the EM gate to a higher (more 'open') value in the DM and NM conditions (where there are gaps in the model's understanding of the ongoing situation, causing it to be uncertain about what was coming next), and it suppresses episodic retrieval in the RM condition (where there are no gaps).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EM gate data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Within the DM condition, the model sets the EM gate to a higher value when the feature controlling the next transition has not been recently observed vs. if the relevant feature has been recently observed.
claims.source: Likewise, within the DM condition, the model sets the EM gate to a higher value when the feature controlling the next transition has not been recently observed (i.e., the feature is not in working memory, causing the model to be uncertain about what was coming next) vs. if the relevant feature has been recently observed and is therefore active in working memory (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EM gate data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: For later time points in part 2, the EM gate is set to a lower value in the DM condition than the NM condition because episodic retrieval that occurs on earlier time points makes the model more certain on later time points.
claims.source: The same principle also explains why, for later time points in part 2, the EM gate is set to a lower value in the DM condition than the NM condition (Figure 3C) – in the DM condition, episodic retrieval that occurs on earlier time points makes the model more certain on later time points, reducing the demand for episodic retrieval and (consequently) leading to lower EM gate values.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EM gate data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: When the model is unsure about what will happen next, the potential benefits of episodic retrieval are high.
claims.source: The fact that the model learned a demand-sensitive retrieval policy can be explained in terms of a simple cost-benefit analysis: When the model is unsure about what will happen next, the potential benefits of episodic retrieval are high.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the model's learned policy.

claims.claim: When the feature of the situation that controls the transition is already in working memory, there is less of a benefit associated with episodic retrieval.
claims.source: By contrast, when the feature of the situation that controls the transition is already in working memory (and consequently the model is able to make a specific prediction about what will happen next), there is less of a benefit associated with episodic retrieval
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the cost-benefit tradeoff of retrieval.

claims.claim: When the correct feature is in working memory, there is a potential cost to retrieving from episodic memory: Lures are always present, and if the model recalls a lure this can overwrite the correct information in working memory.
claims.source: Furthermore, in this scenario, there is also a potential cost to retrieving from episodic memory: Lures are always present, and if the model recalls a lure this can overwrite the correct information in working memory.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the risks of retrieval.

claims.claim: The potential costs of episodic retrieval outweigh the benefits in the 'high certainty' scenario, so the model learns a policy of waiting to retrieve until it is uncertain.
claims.source: Since the potential costs of episodic retrieval outweigh the benefits of episodic retrieval in the 'high certainty' scenario, the model learns a policy of waiting to retrieve until it is uncertain about what will happen next.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the model's learned policy.

claims.claim: The norm of activity in the decision layer is lower when the model is uncertain vs. certain.
claims.source: we investigated this and found that the norm of activity in the decision layer is lower when the model is uncertain vs. certain (for more details, see Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis results reported in Appendix 1.

claims.claim: A version of the model without the 'don't know' option can still show demand-sensitive retrieval.
claims.source: In other simulations (reported in Appendix 5), we found that a version of the model without the 'don't know' option can still leverage this implicit neural correlate of certainty to show demand-sensitive retrieval (i.e., more episodic retrieval in the DM condition than the RM condition)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results reported in Appendix 5.

claims.claim: The main effect of including the 'don't know' option is to make the model more patient overall, by reducing the cost associated with waiting to retrieve from episodic memory.
claims.source: the main effect of including the 'don't know' option is to make the model more patient overall, by reducing the cost associated with waiting to retrieve from episodic memory.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing model variants.

claims.claim: When the penalty is zero, the model makes specific next-state predictions even when it cannot reliably predict the next state, leading to many errors.
claims.source: Our first finding is that adjusting the penalty at test affects the model's tendency to give 'don't know' responses: When the penalty is zero, the model makes specific next-state predictions (i.e., it refrains from using the 'don't know' response) even when it can not reliably predict the next state, leading to many errors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results from varying the penalty parameter.

claims.claim: When the penalty is high, the model makes more 'don't know' responses.
claims.source: In contrast, when the penalty is high, the model makes more 'don't know' responses (in the DM condition, the model responds 'don't know' 15.8% of the time when penalty is set to 4, vs 0.3% of the time when penalty is set to 0).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on 'don't know' response rates.

claims.claim: When the model is tested in an environment where the penalty is high, it waits longer to retrieve from episodic memory, relative to when the penalty at training is lower.
claims.source: We also found that, when the model is tested in an environment where the penalty is high, it waits longer to retrieve from episodic memory, relative to when the penalty at training is lower (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by recall timing data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Waiting longer to retrieve from episodic memory allows the model to observe more features, which helps to disambiguate the present situation from other, related situations and thereby reduces false recall.
claims.source: Waiting longer to retrieve from episodic memory allows the model to observe more features, which helps to disambiguate the present situation from other, related situations and thereby reduces false recall.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the benefits of delayed retrieval.

claims.claim: Waiting longer to retrieve carries an opportunity cost – the model has to forego all of the rewards it would have received from correct prediction if it had recalled the correct memory earlier.
claims.source: However, waiting longer also carries an opportunity cost – the model has to forego all of the rewards it would have received (from correct prediction) if it had recalled the correct memory earlier.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the costs of delayed retrieval.

claims.claim: When the penalty is low, the benefits of retrieving early outweigh the costs, but when the penalty is high, the costs outweigh the benefits, so the model is more cautious.
claims.source: When the penalty is low, the benefits of retrieving early (in terms of increased correct prediction) outweigh the costs (in terms of increased incorrect prediction due to false recall), but when the penalty is high, the costs outweigh the benefits, so the model is more cautious and it waits to observe more features to be sure that the memory it (eventually) recalls is the right one.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the speed-accuracy tradeoff in the model.

claims.claim: Half of the time points were schematic in the schema strength simulations.
claims.source: To explore the effects of schema strength, we ran simulations where half of the time points were schematic.
claims.evidence: This claim describes the simulation design for schema strength experiments.

claims.claim: For non-schematic time points, all of the states associated with that time point were equally probable.
claims.source: For the other half of the time points (non-schematic time points), all of the states associated with that time point were equally probable (given that there were four possible states at each time point, the probability of each state was 0.25).
claims.evidence: This claim describes the simulation design for non-schematic time points.

claims.claim: For high levels of schema strength, episodic retrieval is suppressed for schematic time points and elevated for non-schematic time points.
claims.source: The first thing to note about these results is that, for high levels of schema strength, episodic retrieval is suppressed for schematic time points (i.e., time points with a prototypical state) and elevated for non-schematic time points (i.e., time points where there was not a prototypical state).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EM gate data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: High-schema-strength states are almost fully predictable without episodic memory, so there is no need to retrieve from episodic memory.
claims.source: The former finding (suppression of retrieval at time points where there is a strong prototype) fits with the intuition, noted above, that high-schema-strength states are almost fully predictable without episodic memory, and thus there is no need to retrieve from episodic memory.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about why retrieval is suppressed for schematic states.

claims.claim: Schema-congruent features tend to be shared by both target and lure memories and thus are not diagnostic of which memory is the target.
claims.source: The latter finding (enhanced retrieval at non-schematic time points, when schema strength is high overall) can be explained in terms of the idea that schema-congruent features tend to be shared by both target and lure memories and thus are not diagnostic of which memory is the target
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about memory diagnosticity.

claims.claim: The only way to distinguish between targets and lures when schema strength is high is to recall non-schematic features, which is why the model tries extra-hard to retrieve them from episodic memory.
claims.source: in this situation, the only way to distinguish between targets and lures is to recall non-schematic features, which is why the model tries extra-hard to retrieve them from episodic memory.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the model's retrieval strategy.

claims.claim: When schema strength = .55 or .65, the model shows the opposite pattern: episodic retrieval is enhanced for schematic time points and suppressed for non-schematic time points.
claims.source: Interestingly, the model shows the opposite pattern of effects when schema strength = .55 or .65: Episodic retrieval is enhanced for schematic time points and suppressed for non-schematic time points.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EM gate data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: When schema strength = .55 or .65, the model has started to build up a tendency to guess the schema-congruent state, but it is also going to be wrong about 1/3 of the time, incurring a substantial penalty.
claims.source: This reversal can be explained as follows: When schema strength = .55 or .65, the model has started to build up a tendency to guess the schema-congruent (prototypical) state, but it is also going to be wrong about 1/3 of the time when it guesses the schema-congruent state, incurring a substantial penalty.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the model's behavior at intermediate schema strengths.

claims.claim: To counteract the tendency to make wrong guesses at intermediate schema strengths, the model needs to try extra-hard to retrieve the actual feature value for schematic time points.
claims.source: To counteract this tendency to make wrong guesses, the model needs to try extra-hard to retrieve the actual feature value for schematic time points (which is why the EM gate value increases for these time points)
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the model's compensatory strategy.

claims.claim: The model is more cautious about retrieving from episodic memory if trained in environments where memories are highly similar.
claims.source: With regard to similarity: We found that the model is more cautious about retrieving from episodic memory if trained in environments where memories are highly similar (because the risk of false recall is higher) – see Appendix 2 for details.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results reported in Appendix 2.

claims.claim: When provided with a familiarity signal that is informative about whether a situation was previously encountered, the model learns to exploit this information by retrieving more from episodic memory when the familiarity signal is high.
claims.source: With regard to familiarity: When we provided the model with a familiarity signal that is informative about whether a situation was previously encountered, we found that the model learns to exploit this information by retrieving more from episodic memory when the familiarity signal is high and retrieving less from episodic memory when the familiarity signal is low.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results reported in Appendix 3.

claims.claim: The model provides a resource-rational account of experimental findings showing that familiar stimuli shift the hippocampus into a 'retrieval mode'.
claims.source: This result provides a resource-rational account of experimental findings showing that familiar stimuli shift the hippocampus into a 'retrieval mode' where it is more likely to (subsequently) retrieve episodic memories (Duncan et al., 2012; Duncan and Shohamy, 2016; Duncan et al., 2019; Patil and Duncan, 2018; Hasselmo and Wyble, 1997; Hasselmo et al., 1995)
claims.evidence: This claim relates model results to empirical findings from cited studies.

claims.claim: A selective encoding policy can benefit performance by reducing interference at retrieval later on.
claims.source: Here, we shift our focus to the complementary question of encoding policy: When is the best time to store episodic memories? In the simulations reported below, we show that a selective encoding policy can benefit performance, by reducing interference at retrieval later on.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results on encoding policies.

claims.claim: The model is presently not capable of learning an encoding policy on its own.
claims.source: Note that our model is presently not capable of learning an encoding policy on its own (see Discussion)
claims.evidence: This claim describes a limitation of the current model.

claims.claim: The hippocampal response tends to peak at event boundaries.
claims.source: These studies found that the hippocampal response tends to peak at event boundaries (Ben-Yakov and Dudai, 2011; Ben-Yakov et al., 2013; Baldassano et al., 2017; Ben-Yakov and Henson, 2018; Reagh et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple fMRI studies.

claims.claim: The boundary-locked hippocampal response predicts subsequent memory performance for the just-completed event.
claims.source: this boundary-locked response predicts subsequent memory performance for the just-completed event (Ben-Yakov and Dudai, 2011; Baldassano et al., 2017; Reagh et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: The boundary-locked hippocampal response is a neural signature of episodic encoding of the just-completed event.
claims.source: leading researchers to conclude that it is a neural signature of episodic encoding of the just-completed event.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited empirical findings.

claims.claim: Information about the current situation builds up in working memory within an event, and then is 'flushed out' at event boundaries.
claims.source: Several researchers have argued that information about the current situation builds up in working memory within an event, and then is 'flushed out' at event boundaries (Radvansky et al., 2011; Richmond and Zacks, 2017; for neural evidence in support of this dynamic, see Ezzyat and Davachi, 2011; Chien and Honey, 2020; Ezzyat and Davachi, 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claims.claim: The model's representation of the features of an event will be most complete right before the end of the event, making this a particularly advantageous time to take an episodic memory snapshot.
claims.source: This dynamic (which is illustrated in the model in Figure 2C) means that the model's representation of the features of an event will be most complete right before the end of the event, making this a particularly advantageous time to take an episodic memory snapshot of the situation model.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the model's dynamics shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Models that encode an additional episodic memory midway through each event performed worse in the DM condition during part 2.
claims.source: Our simulation shows that in the DM condition, during part 2, models that encode an additional episodic memory midway through each event performed worse (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by performance data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: When midway memories are also stored, midway memories of the target event are recalled more strongly than memories formed at the end of the target event.
claims.source: First, as shown in Figure 4B, when midway memories are also stored, midway memories of the target event are recalled more strongly than memories formed at the end of the target event.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by memory activation data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The model's hidden state strongly encodes temporal context: WM states stored at similar times within an event tend to be more similar than WM states stored at different times.
claims.source: This advantage occurs because the model's hidden state strongly encodes temporal context: WM states stored at similar times within an event tend to be more similar than WM states stored at different times (this illustrated by Figure 4E, which shows that time information within an event is more strongly represented than differences across events).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Early on in part 2 of the event, the temporal context represented in working memory will be a better match for memories encoded midway through the event than memories encoded at the end of the event.
claims.source: One consequence of this time coding is that – early on in part 2 of the event (when the benefits of episodic retrieval are the largest) – the temporal context represented in working memory will be a better match for memories encoded midway through the event than memories encoded at the end of the event (Figure 4C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from similarity data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claims.claim: The temporal context match provides a competitive advantage for the midway memory over the endpoint memory, resulting in the midway memory blocking the endpoint memory from coming strongly to mind.
claims.source: This temporal context match provides a competitive advantage for the midway memory over the endpoint memory, resulting in the midway memory blocking the endpoint memory from coming strongly to mind.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the retrieval dynamics.

claims.claim: The midway memory is less informative because it contains fewer features of the situation.
claims.source: The second key point is that the midway memory is less informative (i.e., it contains fewer features of the situation, because it was stored before the full set of features was observed).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the information content of midway memories.

claims.claim: Recalling the midway target memory confers less of a benefit on future prediction than recalling the endpoint memory would have provided.
claims.source: As such, recalling the midway target memory confers less of a benefit on future prediction than recalling the endpoint memory would have provided – this is the main reason why prediction is worse in the midway condition.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about why midway encoding harms performance.

claims.claim: Because midway memories contain less information, they are more confusable across events.
claims.source: The third key point is that, because midway memories contain less information, they are more confusable across events (i.e., it is harder to determine which event the memory pertains to).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the distinctiveness of midway memories.

claims.claim: Midway lures tend to become more active at retrieval than endpoint lures.
claims.source: As a result, midway lures tend to become more active at retrieval than endpoint lures (Figure 4B)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by memory activation data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In a version of the model where memories were stored both midway and at the end of an event during meta-training, endpoint-only encoding still led to better performance than midway-plus-endpoint encoding.
claims.source: To address this concern, we also ran a version of the model where memories were stored both midway and at the end of an event during meta-training, and it was still true that endpoint-only encoding led to better performance than midway-plus-endpoint encoding
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by additional simulation results.

claims.claim: Midway encoding is intrinsically harmful, and it is not just a matter of it being out-of-distribution.
claims.source: this result shows that midway encoding is intrinsically harmful, and it is not just a matter of it being out-of-distribution.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the additional simulation results.

claims.claim: The harmful effect of encoding midway through the sequence qualitatively replicates with more complex event structures where queries are repeated within a sequence.
claims.source: In another simulation, we also found that the harmful effect of encoding midway through the sequence qualitatively replicates with more complex event structures (analogous to those in Botvinick and Plaut, 2004) where queries are repeated within a sequence and the model has to give a different response to the first vs. second occurrence of a query (e.g., mood is controlled first by weather and later by music).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by additional simulation results with more complex structures.

claims.claim: The model does better when forced to wait until the end of an event to take a snapshot.
claims.source: To summarize the results from this section, the model does better when we force it to wait until the end of an event to take a snapshot.
claims.evidence: This claim summarizes the results from the encoding policy simulations.

claims.claim: This pattern arises because knowledge of the ongoing situation builds within an event, so memories encoded earlier in the event contain less information than memories encoded at the end.
claims.source: This pattern arises in our simulations because knowledge of the ongoing situation builds within an event, so memories encoded earlier in the event contain less information about the situation than memories encoded at the end.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about why endpoint encoding is beneficial.

claims.claim: Less-informative midway memories harm performance by interfering with recall of more-informative endpoint memories, and are themselves more prone to false recall.
claims.source: These less-informative midway memories harm performance by interfering with recall of more-informative endpoint memories, and are themselves more prone to false recall (because they are more confusable across events).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the simulation results.

claims.claim: The simulation results provide a resource-rational justification for results showing preferential encoding-related hippocampal activity at the end of events.
claims.source: Taken together, these simulation results provide a resource-rational justification for the results cited above showing preferential encoding-related hippocampal activity at the end of events (Ben-Yakov and Dudai, 2011; Ben-Yakov et al., 2013; Baldassano et al., 2017; Ben-Yakov and Henson, 2018; Reagh et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim relates the simulation results to empirical findings from cited studies.

claims.claim: The modeling work leverages recent advances in memory-augmented neural networks, deep reinforcement learning, and meta-learning.
claims.source: Our modeling work leverages recent advances in memory-augmented neural networks (Graves et al., 2016; Ritter et al., 2018), deep reinforcement learning (Mnih et al., 2016; Sutton and Barto, 2018), and meta-learning (Wang et al., 2018; Botvinick et al., 2019)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant technical advances.

claims.claim: These advances make it possible for neural network models to learn to use episodic memory in the service of prediction.
claims.source: these advances (collectively) make it possible for neural network models to learn to use episodic memory in the service of prediction (for an earlier precedent, see Zilli and Hasselmo, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the capabilities enabled by the cited technical advances.

claims.claim: The episodic memory system used in the model is similar to recently-described memory-augmented neural networks with a differentiable neural dictionary (DND).
claims.source: Conceptually, the episodic memory system used in our model is similar to recently-described memory-augmented neural networks with a differentiable neural dictionary (DND) (Pritzel et al., 2017; Ritter et al., 2018; Ritter, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim relates the model to prior work with citations.

claims.claim: In DND models, each memory is a key-value pair where keys define the similarity metric across all memories and values represent the content of these memories.
claims.source: In these models, the data structure of the episodic memory system is dictionary-like: Each memory is a key-value pair. The keys define the similarity metric across all memories, and the values represent the content of these memories.
claims.evidence: This claim describes the structure of DND models based on cited literature.

claims.claim: Ritter et al., 2018 was the first paper to use the DND for cognitive modeling and served as a major inspiration for the work presented here.
claims.source: Ritter et al., 2018 is particularly relevant as it was the first paper (to our knowledge) to use the DND for cognitive modeling and – as such – served as a major inspiration for the work presented here (see also Botvinick et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim acknowledges the influence of prior work with citation.

claims.claim: The way the model uses the DND mechanism is quite similar to how it was used in Ritter et al., 2018.
claims.source: The way that our model uses the DND mechanism is quite similar to how it was used in Ritter et al., 2018
claims.evidence: This claim compares the current model to prior work.

claims.claim: The idea that the neocortical network learns to control a 'gate' on episodic retrieval via reinforcement learning was taken from Ritter et al., 2018.
claims.source: in particular, we took from the Ritter et al., 2018 paper the idea that the neocortical network learns to control a 'gate' on episodic retrieval via reinforcement learning (for an earlier model that also used reinforcement learning to learn a policy for retrieval from episodic memory, see Zilli and Hasselmo, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim acknowledges the source of a key modeling idea with citations.

claims.claim: In the current model, the gate controls the flow of information into the episodic memory module (pre-gating), but in the Ritter model the gate controls the flow of information out of the episodic memory module (post-gating).
claims.source: The most salient difference regards the placement of the EM gate: In our model, the gate controls the flow of information into the episodic memory module (pre-gating), but in the Ritter model the gate controls the flow of information out of the episodic memory module (post-gating).
claims.evidence: This claim describes a key architectural difference between models.

claims.claim: The key simulation results qualitatively replicate in a version of the model that uses post-gating.
claims.source: While this is a major difference, we found that our key simulation results qualitatively replicate in a version of the model that uses post-gating, indicating that the selective encoding and retrieval principles discussed here do not depend on the exact placement of the gate (see Appendix 4 for simulation results and more discussion of these points).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results reported in Appendix 4.

claims.claim: The model's computation of which memories are retrieved is more complex than in Ritter et al., 2018.
claims.source: Another difference is that our model's computation of which memories are retrieved (given a particular retrieval cue, assuming that the 'gate' on retrieval is open) is more complex.
claims.evidence: This claim describes a difference in model architecture.

claims.claim: Ritter et al., 2018 used a one-nearest-neighbor matching algorithm during recall.
claims.source: Ritter et al., 2018 used a one-nearest-neighbor matching algorithm during recall, whereby the stored memory with the highest match to the cue is selected for retrieval (assuming that the gate is open).
claims.evidence: This claim describes the retrieval mechanism in the cited model.

claims.claim: Memory activation in the current model is computed using a competitive evidence accumulation process, in line with prior cognitive models of retrieval.
claims.source: By contrast, memory activation in our model is computed using a competitive evidence accumulation process, in line with prior cognitive models of retrieval (e.g., Polyn et al., 2009; Sederberg et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim describes the retrieval mechanism with citations to prior cognitive models.

claims.claim: The addition of the 'don't know' output unit is a structural difference between the current model and the Ritter et al., 2018 model.
claims.source: A third structural difference between our model and the Ritter et al., 2018 model is our addition of the 'don't know' output unit, which (when selected) allows the model to avoid both reward and punishment.
claims.evidence: This claim describes a difference in model architecture.

claims.claim: The main difference between the current modeling work and Ritter et al., 2018 relates to the application domain.
claims.source: Apart from the structural differences noted above, the main difference between our modeling work and the work done by Ritter et al., 2018 relates to the application domain (i.e., which cognitive phenomena were simulated).
claims.evidence: This claim compares the scope of the two modeling efforts.

claims.claim: The current modeling work focused on how episodic memory can support incidental prediction of upcoming states, when there is no explicit demand for a decision.
claims.source: Our modeling work in this paper focused on how episodic memory can support incidental prediction of upcoming states, when there is no explicit demand for a decision.
claims.evidence: This claim describes the focus of the current work.

claims.claim: Ritter et al., 2018 focused on how episodic memory can be used to support performance in classic decision-making tasks.
claims.source: By contrast, Ritter et al., 2018 focused on how episodic memory can be used to support performance in classic decision-making tasks, such as bandit tasks and maze learning, that have been extensively explored in the reinforcement learning literature.
claims.evidence: This claim describes the focus of the cited work.

claims.claim: The structured event memory (SEM) model uses RNNs to represent its knowledge of schemas.
claims.source: Like our model, SEM uses RNNs to represent its knowledge of schemas (i.e., how events typically unfold).
claims.evidence: This claim describes a similarity between models with citation.

claims.claim: SEM records episodic memory traces as it processes events.
claims.source: Also, like our model, SEM records episodic memory traces as it processes events.
claims.evidence: This claim describes another similarity between models.

claims.claim: The current model uses a single RNN to represent a single (contextually parameterized) schema, whereas SEM uses multiple RNNs that each represent a distinct schema.
claims.source: First, whereas our model uses a single RNN to represent a single (contextually parameterized) schema, SEM uses multiple RNNs that each represent a distinct schema for how events can unfold.
claims.evidence: This claim describes a key difference between the models.

claims.claim: SEM contains specialized computational machinery that allows it to determine which of its stored schemas is relevant at a particular moment, and also when it is appropriate to instantiate a new schema.
claims.source: Building on prior work on nonparametric Bayesian inference (Anderson, 1991; Aldous, 1983; Pitman, 2006) and latent cause modeling (Gershman et al., 2010; Gershman et al., 2015), SEM contains specialized computational machinery that allows it to determine which of its stored schemas (each with its own RNN) is relevant at a particular moment, and also when it is appropriate to instantiate a new schema (with its own, new RNN) to learn about ongoing events.

results.result: The authors developed a memory-augmented neural network model with neocortical and hippocampal components that implements working memory (via LSTM), semantic memory (via connection weights), and episodic memory (via snapshot storage and LCA-based retrieval). The model learns retrieval policies through reinforcement learning with a meta-learning procedure.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C21-C45 collectively describe the model architecture and training procedure. The model design is clearly specified with appropriate citations to prior methods (LSTM, LCA, meta-learning), and the training procedure using reinforcement learning with a 'don't know' option is well-documented. The architecture is illustrated in Figure 1 and the methodological choices are justified.

results.result: The model learned a demand-sensitive retrieval policy: it retrieves more from episodic memory when uncertain about upcoming states (DM condition) and suppresses retrieval when information is maintained in working memory (RM condition). This pattern qualitatively matches empirical findings from Chen et al., 2016 showing stronger hippocampal-neocortical coupling in the DM condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C17, C87-C107 are supported by simulation data shown in Figures 3A-D. The model shows higher memory activation and EM gate values in the DM condition compared to RM condition, matching the empirical pattern. The cost-benefit analysis explanation (C101-C104) is logically coherent and supported by the model's learned behavior. The finding that uncertainty correlates with decision layer activity norm (C105) provides a mechanistic basis for the policy.

results.result: The model's retrieval policy adapts to penalty levels: with high penalties for incorrect predictions, the model waits longer to retrieve from episodic memory and makes more 'don't know' responses, implementing a speed-accuracy tradeoff.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C113 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E. The model demonstrates flexible adjustment of retrieval timing based on penalty levels, with clear quantitative differences in 'don't know' response rates (15.8% vs 0.3%). The speed-accuracy tradeoff explanation is logically sound and consistent with the model's reward structure.

results.result: Schema strength modulates retrieval policy in a non-monotonic way: at high schema strength, retrieval is suppressed for schematic time points but enhanced for non-schematic time points; at intermediate schema strength (0.55-0.65), the pattern reverses.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C122 are supported by simulation data in Figure 3G. The non-monotonic relationship between schema strength and retrieval is clearly demonstrated. The explanations for both patterns (C117-C119 for high schema strength, C121-C122 for intermediate) are logically coherent, though the intermediate pattern is somewhat complex and could benefit from additional validation.

results.result: The model shows increased caution in retrieving from episodic memory when trained in environments with highly similar memories, and learns to exploit familiarity signals by retrieving more when familiarity is high.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C125 are supported by simulation results reported in Appendices 2 and 3. The familiarity result (C124-C125) provides a resource-rational account of empirical findings with appropriate citations. However, these results are in appendices and less central to the main narrative.

results.result: Encoding episodic memories selectively at event endpoints (rather than also mid-event) leads to better prediction performance. This occurs because midway memories are less informative, interfere with endpoint memory retrieval due to temporal context matching, and are more prone to false recall.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C126-C148 are supported by simulation data in Figure 4. The performance decrement with midway encoding is clearly shown (Figure 4A), and the three mechanistic explanations (temporal context advantage for midway memories, lower information content, higher confusability) are each supported by data (Figures 4B-E). The control simulation (C142-C143) addresses the out-of-distribution concern. This provides a resource-rational account of empirical findings on boundary-locked hippocampal activity (C128-C130, C148).

results.result: The modeling approach targets the Chen et al., 2016 study, which manipulated episodic memory availability and demand through three conditions (RM, DM, NM) and found stronger hippocampal-neocortical coupling in the DM condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C63 accurately describe the Chen et al., 2016 study design and findings with appropriate citations. The interpretation of the conditions as manipulating memory demand (C54-C58) is reasonable and well-justified. This provides the empirical foundation for the modeling work.

results.result: The training environment consists of events defined as sequences of states sampled from an event schema, where situation features deterministically control state transitions. The model observes features in random order and predicts upcoming states. The simulation implements the three conditions from Chen et al., 2016 with appropriate manipulations of working memory and episodic memory availability.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C83 describe the task environment and simulation design. The task structure is clearly specified with appropriate parameters (C71: 16 time points, 4 states per time point). The implementation of the three experimental conditions (C77-C82) appropriately captures the key features of the Chen et al., 2016 design. The encoding policy (C75-C76) is imposed by hand based on prior empirical findings, which is acknowledged as a limitation (C127).

results.result: Decoding analysis of the model's working memory state shows that observed features are actively maintained until the end of an event, the situation representation becomes more complete over time, and episodic retrieval early in part 2 reinstates features before they are re-observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 2C. The decoding accuracy of 91.58% indicates the analysis is reliable. The visualization clearly shows feature maintenance, accumulation, and retrieval-based reinstatement. This provides important validation of the model's internal dynamics.

results.result: The modeling approach leverages recent advances in memory-augmented neural networks (particularly the DND mechanism from Ritter et al., 2018), deep reinforcement learning, and meta-learning. Key differences from Ritter et al., 2018 include pre-gating vs post-gating, competitive evidence accumulation for retrieval, the 'don't know' option, and focus on incidental prediction rather than decision-making tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C164 accurately describe the technical foundations and relationship to prior work with appropriate citations. The comparison to Ritter et al., 2018 is thorough and fair, acknowledging both similarities and differences. The finding that key results replicate with post-gating (C157) strengthens the conclusions. The discussion appropriately credits the inspiration from prior work while clarifying the novel contributions.

results.result: The current model and the SEM model (Franklin et al., 2020) have complementary strengths: SEM handles multiple schemas and event segmentation but doesn't use episodic memory for online prediction, while the current model uses episodic memory for online prediction but only handles a single schema with imposed event boundaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C179 provide a fair and accurate comparison to the SEM model with appropriate citations. The complementary strengths are clearly articulated (C177-C178), and the speculation about combining the models (C179) is reasonable. This comparison helps position the current work within the broader modeling landscape.

results.result: The model cannot currently learn encoding policies, though this should be possible in principle. Future work could explore how surprise and predictive certainty modulate encoding, as suggested by empirical findings showing enhanced memory for surprising events and reduced encoding for highly predictable events.
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C196 acknowledge a limitation (C180) and discuss future directions. The speculation that encoding policies should be learnable (C181) is reasonable given the results on selective encoding benefits (C4, C126-C148), but this remains untested. The discussion of surprise and certainty as potential encoding modulators (C185-C196) is well-grounded in empirical literature with extensive citations, but the relationship between surprise and event boundaries is noted as complex (C189-C191). This represents promising future work rather than current results.

results.result: The model has several acknowledged limitations and simplifications: memories are stored as distinct entities without updating (C197), only one schema is handled (C209), events have single timescales (C212), and the model uses simplified neural mechanisms (C203). The policies explored focus on when to encode/retrieve rather than what to encode or how to cue memory (C217-C218). Despite these limitations, the model provides initial evidence that selective encoding/retrieval policies can improve performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C197-C228 provide an honest and thorough discussion of limitations with appropriate context. The authors acknowledge simplifications for parsimony and computational tractability (C206-C207, C214), discuss potential extensions with relevant citations (C198-C205, C210, C213, C215-C216), and appropriately characterize the scope of the current work (C220-C225). The finding that frequent encoding can harm performance (C227) has implications for machine learning applications (C226, C228).

results.result: Prior research shows selective episodic encoding and retrieval in naturalistic contexts, but existing computational models focus on list-learning paradigms and don't address when encoding/retrieval should occur. Recent studies using naturalistic stimuli show encoding at event boundaries and retrieval when uncertain.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C13 accurately characterize prior research with extensive appropriate citations. The gap in existing computational models (C8-C9) is correctly identified and motivates the current work. The empirical findings on selective encoding/retrieval (C11-C13) provide the phenomena to be explained.

results.result: The model aims to capture neocortical-hippocampal interactions and provide a resource-rational account of when episodic memories should be encoded and retrieved. The key insight is that selective policies help mitigate the risk of retrieving irrelevant memories while retaining episodic memory benefits.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16, C18-C20, C5 articulate the modeling goals and key theoretical insight. The resource-rational framework is appropriate for addressing the 'when' questions about memory use. The risk-mitigation explanation (C19-C20, C5) is consistently supported across multiple results (retrieval policy, encoding policy, penalty effects, schema effects).

results.result: The modeling work builds on the view that episodic memory is a flexible resource used in concert with working memory and semantic memory. The model provides predictions about how episodic memory should be deployed as a function of environmental properties and can spur a cycle of predictions, experiments, and model revision.
results.evaluation: Claims C229-C233 appropriately frame the broader significance of the work with relevant citations. The emphasis on studying memory systems in interaction (C230) rather than isolation is well-justified. The hope for a virtuous cycle of modeling and experimentation (C233) is reasonable given the testable predictions generated.

results.result: The episodic retrieval mechanism uses content-based matching (cosine similarity) with competitive evidence accumulation (LCA). The EM gate controls retrieval strength, and competition level adjusts the contrast across memories. The model learns to control the EM gate via reinforcement learning rather than having parameters hand-tuned to fit data.
results.evaluation: Claims C234-C248 provide detailed specification of the retrieval mechanism. The use of cosine similarity (C236) and LCA with competition (C238-C242) is clearly described. The choice to set competition to 0.8 (C243) is justified by prior evidence for competitive retrieval (C244). The learning-based approach to setting the EM gate (C245-C247) is a strength compared to hand-tuning. The simplifications to the LCA (C248) are acknowledged.
